leads_to.evidence: BLS lists a doctoral or professional degree as the typical entry education for biochemists. Biological sciences majors make up most U.S. medical school applicants, so first-year pay understates many graduates who are still in school.

nearby_pair.evidence: Both are traditional four-year residential biochemistry bachelor's programs that admit first-year students. USC runs its BS jointly between biology and chemistry, and Occidental runs an interdisciplinary major built on research.

school_matters.evidence: Pay barely changes with selectivity. Research biochemist jobs require a Ph.D., and a bachelor's qualifies a graduate for only some entry-level lab roles, so first jobs pay about the same from any school.

who_is_counted.evidence: The largest programs have no online-only offerings and admit students as freshmen at research universities, so their graduates are mostly new graduates, not working adults finishing a degree. I did not check each program's admission page.

programs.evidence: The Oakland campus reports the same figures as Northeastern's Boston campus, so its numbers appear to be pooled with Boston's rather than measured on its own.
Northeastern's highly selective biochemistry BS builds paid co-op terms into the degree, and students have worked at pharmaceutical companies in Cambridge before graduating.
CSUSM sits in San Diego County, which it calls a worldwide biotech hub with over a thousand companies. Its alumni work at local employers such as Illumina and Thermo Fisher.
